name: ai_lobbying_spend_2026
document:
# How much was paid to lobby on artificial intelligence in 2026

## The question

Across the Senate LDA disclosures for Q1 and Q2 2026, how much did clients pay outside
lobbying firms to lobby on artificial intelligence?

## The corpus

Two exports, read exactly as filed: `lda_data_Q1_2026.xlsx` and `lda_data_Q2_2026.xlsx`.
Every Senate LDA filing here is real and public record, not a sample. Each
carries one row per filing per issue area, so a filing that lobbied on three issue
areas is three rows stating the same money once each.

## Step 1 - find the rows that mention AI

Search each row's own `specific_issues` and `issue_codes` for six terms, on word
boundaries, ignoring case: artificial intelligence, AI, machine learning, large language
model (and LLM), deepfake, algorithmic. This is a net, not a judgement: it catches
algorithmic trading and airline codes on purpose, and leaves the deciding to step 2.

Every row that matches none of the six is dropped and enters no figure. A filing that
lobbied on AI without using one of these terms is outside what this run can see.

## Step 2 - judge whether the filing is really about AI

Ask a model, one row at a time, whether the filing's own issue text says the lobbying was
about artificial intelligence - its regulation, funding, procurement, or its use in some
sector - or whether the term is incidental. It answers with a verdict and a one-sentence
basis quoting the text it decided on. A row with no verdict is dropped: no verdict is not
a yes.

## Step 3 - read the money as filed

Read `income` and `expenses` as plain dollar numbers. Blank counts as zero: the filing is
reporting it received or spent nothing. Anything else that is not a plain number, and any
negative amount, stops the run rather than being interpreted.

## Step 4 - separate paid lobbying from in-house

A filing whose type begins with `Registration` is a registration. A filing whose
registrant and client are the same name as filed is in-house. Everything else is one
organisation paying another. Names are compared exactly as filed; nothing here merges two
spellings of one organisation.

## Step 5 - one row per filing

Collapse the surviving rows to one per `filing_uuid`. A column the rows of one filing
disagree on stops the run rather than being picked from; the per-issue-area fields are
carried as lists.

## Step 6 - a person confirms every paid filing

Before anything is published, every paid filing the model read as being about AI is put
in front of a person, largest reported spend first. They confirm or overturn the
model's reading; overturning one drops the filing from every figure below.

## The published figures

Over the paid filings a person confirmed: the reported income summed exactly as filed,
the filings behind it, and the distinct firms and clients. In-house spending is reported
separately, on the model's reading alone, and is never added to it.

llm.prompt_instructions:
You are reading one row of a US Senate lobbying disclosure (an LDA filing), for a newsroom building a public figure: how much was paid to lobby on artificial intelligence in 2026.

A keyword scan already found an AI term in this row's issue text. That scan cannot tell "we lobbied on the AI Act" from "we lobbied on Medicare; also AI in radiology came up" from a false positive like an airline code or "Bahrain (AI)". Deciding which of those this is, is your whole job.

Your answer decides whether this filing's reported dollars enter the published total. A reviewer sees your verdict and your basis next to the filing's own issue text, and can overrule either. Nothing else about the run is shown to you: not the amount, not the client's size, not what any other filing was judged. Judge the text in front of you.

Return a JSON object with exactly these two fields:

1. "is_about_ai": true when the filing's own issue text says this lobbying was about artificial intelligence — its regulation, funding, procurement, or its use in some sector. false when the AI term is incidental, is part of an unrelated name or code, or the text does not support the reading.

2. "ai_basis": one short sentence, quoting or naming the part of the issue text you decided on. Where you answered false, say what the term turned out to be.

Worked example. Issue text: "H.R. 5628, the Artificial Intelligence Accountability Act; oversight of automated decision systems in hiring." →
{"is_about_ai": true, "ai_basis": "Names the Artificial Intelligence Accountability Act and oversight of automated hiring decisions."}

queue.reviewer_instructions:
This client paid an outside firm these dollars, and a model read the filing as being about AI. You are deciding whether that reading holds, because these dollars are the published figure.

Approve where the filing's own issue text says the lobbying was about AI — its regulation, funding, procurement, or its use in some sector. Overturn it where the AI term is incidental: a passing mention, an unrelated sense of the word, or one clause in a filing about something else.

Judge the text in front of you. The amount is shown because it says how much rests on the decision, not because a large filing deserves a different answer.
